citation: Brochard L, Mancebo J, Wysocki M, Lofaso F, Conti G, Rauss A, Simonneau G, Benito S, Gasparetto A, Lemaire F, Isabey D, Harf A. Noninvasive ventilation for acute exacerbations of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. N Engl J Med. 1995;333(13):817-822
one_liner: In ICU patients with acute hypercapnic AECOPD, early NIV reduced intubation (26% vs 74%) and in-hospital mortality (9% vs 29%), establishing NIV as first-line ventilatory support.

pico.population: ICU patients with acute exacerbation of COPD and respiratory acidosis (pH <7.35, PaCO2 elevated) not requiring immediate intubation.
pico.intervention: Early face-mask pressure-support NIV (20 cm H2O, no PEEP, ≥6h/day) plus standard medical therapy.
pico.comparison: Standard medical therapy alone: oxygen via nasal prongs (max 5 L/min) to keep SpO2 >90%.
pico.outcome: Need for endotracheal intubation (primary); in-hospital mortality, complications, hospital length of stay.

background.existing_knowledge: AECOPD with hypercapnic acidosis often leads to intubation and invasive ventilation with risks of complications.
background.knowledge_gap: Whether NIV could reduce intubation and improve outcomes in ICU patients with AECOPD was unclear.
background.hypothesis: Early NIV plus standard therapy would reduce the need for endotracheal intubation compared with standard therapy alone.

methods.design: Multicentre RCT (5 ICUs, 3 countries) with parallel groups.
methods.setting: ICUs in France, Italy, Spain; screened 275 admissions, enrolled 85.

inclusion: Known COPD (or high probability) with exacerbation <2 weeks
At least 2 of: respiratory rate >30/min, PaO2 <45 mmHg, pH <7.35 after 10 min room air
exclusion: Immediate intubation requirement (respiratory arrest, severe haemodynamic instability, mask intolerance, impaired consciousness, airway clearance issues, high aspiration risk)
Alternative cause (septic shock, MI, pneumothorax, PE, severe pneumonia, recent surgery/trauma)

methods.intervention: Pressure-support ventilation via face mask, starting pressure support 20 cm H2O (adjusted for comfort), expiratory pressure at atmospheric (no PEEP), FiO2 to maintain SpO2>90%, delivered ≥6 h/day with up to 2 h spontaneous breathing, duration by clinical/ABG criteria.
methods.comparison: Standard therapy: oxygen via nasal prongs (max 5 L/min) to SpO2>90%, plus protocolised medical therapy. Predefined intubation criteria applied after 1 h of assigned treatment; in NIV arm, a step of NIV resumption before intubation was allowed if criteria met.
secondary_outcomes: Proportion of patients with ≥1 complication not present on admission
methods.follow_up: In-hospital through discharge or death; spirometry and ABG within 3 months after discharge.

headline_bullets: Intubation: 11/43 (26%) with NIV vs 31/42 (74%) with standard therapy (P<0.001).
In-hospital mortality: 4/43 (9%) vs 12/42 (29%) (P=0.02), not significant after adjustment for intubation.
Fewer patients developed new complications (7/43, 16% vs 20/42, 48%; P=0.001) and shorter hospital stay (23±17 vs 35±33 days; P=0.02).
Physiological improvements at 1 h: PaCO2 55±9 vs 70±15 mmHg; pH 7.33±0.04 vs 7.27±0.06; respiratory rate 25±8 vs 33±7 breaths/min.

outcomes_table.note: Not significant after adjustment for intubation (Mantel–Haenszel)

outcomes_table.outcome: Patients with ≥1 complication not present on admission
outcomes_table.note: Total complications: 9 vs 23; complications leading to death: 4 vs 12
Subgroup by intubation: no-intubation 17±9 vs 20±16; intubated 40±22 vs 41±36
Reported among complications not present on admission; not associated with death

subgroup_table.subgroup: Intubation status (post-randomisation) – hospital length of stay

safety: Facial-skin necrosis: 1 event in NIV group.
Fewer patients with any new complication: 7/43 (16%) vs 20/42 (48%).

domains.notes: Randomised via sealed envelopes; allocation concealment safeguards not reported.
Unblinded; intubation criteria were predefined to mitigate bias.
Post-randomisation exclusions not reported; 1-h physiological data missing for some due to early intubation (standard N=39, NIV N=42).
NIV delivery required ≥6 h/day; actual adherence not reported. Standard therapy oxygen limit 5 L/min.
Groups similar: pH 7.28 vs 7.27, PaCO2 68 vs 69 mmHg, RR 35 vs 37, SAPS 11 vs 11.
Primary outcome (intubation) is objective and protocolised; complications were clinically assessed and not adjudicated independently.
Two-tailed P<0.05; no pre-specified power calculation; multiple outcomes tested.

internal_validity.verdict: Internal validity is moderate-to-strong given randomisation, baseline balance, protocolised intubation criteria, and large between-group separation, but limited by unblinded design, small sample, and lack of pre-specified power.

domains.notes: Highly selected: 85 of 275 screened enrolled; exclusions for immediate intubation and many alternate diagnoses. Enrolees had severe acidosis (pH ~7.27).
ICU setting with rapid intubation capacity; NIV settings (pressure support without PEEP, SpO2 >90%) differ from contemporary bilevel NIV and controlled oxygen targets.

external_validity.verdict: Generalisability is moderate: directly applicable to ICU patients with AECOPD and severe acidosis not requiring immediate intubation, but less so for mixed aetiologies, ward settings, or patients with immediate airway compromise.

strengths: Multicentre randomised design in ICUs across three countries.
Clinically decisive primary endpoint (intubation) with protocolised criteria.
Rapid and substantial physiological improvement (CO2 clearance, pH) supporting mechanism.
Patient-centred secondary outcomes (mortality, complications, length of stay) captured.
limitations: Unblinded intervention may influence discretionary outcomes (e.g., length of stay, complication recognition).
Small sample size (N=85) with no pre-specified power calculation.
Highly selected population (19% of screened admissions) potentially inflating effect size; control group event rate unusually high.
Ventilation strategy (pressure support without PEEP, liberal oxygen) differs from modern bilevel NIV and controlled oxygen protocols.

critical_appraisal.summary: This is a landmark RCT demonstrating a large treatment effect of NIV on intubation in a highly selected AECOPD population, but unblinded design, small sample, and selection bias limit confidence in the effect size and generalisability to broader practice.

sections.authors_conclusion: In selected patients with AECOPD and acute hypercapnic respiratory acidosis, early NIV significantly reduces the need for intubation, complications, and hospital stay, and is associated with lower mortality.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: NIV is first-line ventilatory support for AECOPD with respiratory acidosis (pH <7.35) in patients who do not require immediate intubation, provided skilled delivery and close monitoring with clear failure criteria are in place.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: ICU or high-acuity monitored settings with rapid escalation capability; patients with severe COPD exacerbation and hypercapnia, no other aetiology requiring immediate intubation.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: NIV can be applied without careful patient selection; failure criteria are still needed, and patients with severe acidosis (pH <7.25) or alternative causes may still require invasive ventilation.
implementation_caveats: Use of bilevel positive airway pressure (IPAP/EPAP) is now standard, not pressure support alone; oxygen targets should be 88–92%.
NIV should be initiated early, within 1 hour of meeting criteria, and patients reassessed frequently; if no improvement in pH, PaCO2, or respiratory rate within 1–2 hours, plan for escalation.
Staff training, appropriate interface, and ready availability of intubation are essential.

controversies.topic: Unblinded design with asymmetric escalation pathways
controversies.notes: The NIV arm included a step of NIV resumption before intubation when criteria were met after NIV withdrawal, which may have biased the intubation outcome.

The intubation rate in the standard therapy group (74%) and mortality (29%) were high, reflecting a severely ill population and era of care; effect size may not translate to modern practice with earlier diagnosis and medical management.
Pressure support without PEEP and oxygen target >90% differ from contemporary bilevel NIV and controlled oxygen protocols; however, the core concept of unloading respiratory muscles remains valid.
Subsequent trials and a Cochrane review (17 trials, N=1264) confirmed reduced mortality (RR 0.54) and intubation (RR 0.36) with NIV in acute hypercapnic AECOPD.
BTS/ICS, ERS/ATS, and ISCCM guidelines all recommend NIV as first-line for AECOPD with pH ≤7.35 and PaCO2 >6.5 kPa, with careful patient selection and monitoring.
Despite evidence, real-world uptake of NIV in AECOPD remains incomplete, with variations in patient selection, team training, and timely escalation, potentially attenuating effectiveness.

context_related_trials.relation: First randomised trial of nasal ventilation in acute ventilatory failure due to COPD, demonstrating feasibility; smaller sample, supported the concept.
Large multicentre trial of NIV in AECOPD on general respiratory wards, extending the evidence to non-ICU settings and showing reduced intubation and mortality.
Meta-analysis of 17 trials (N=1264) confirming NIV reduces mortality (RR 0.54) and intubation (RR 0.36) in acute hypercapnic AECOPD, providing the highest-level evidence supporting practice.

unresolved_questions: Optimal NIV settings (pressure support level, use of PEEP, oxygen targets) in contemporary practice.
Benefit of NIV in less severe acidosis (pH 7.30–7.35) or in patients with mixed aetiologies (e.g., pneumonia).
Strategies to improve adherence to early NIV and timely escalation when it fails, to reduce real-world mortality.

quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: In ICU patients with AECOPD and severe respiratory acidosis, early NIV is the standard of care to avoid intubation and reduce mortality.
